name: Carbon monoxide (CO) alarms
summary: Home alarm that sounds a loud horn when carbon monoxide builds up; plug-in, battery or hardwired, sometimes combined with a smoke alarm.
uses: Warns of CO from any combustion, often before a healthy adult has symptoms; infants, older people and people with heart or lung disease are affected sooner (First Alert CO710; Intertek CSA 6.19)
UL 2034 times, also given for Kidde's CSA 6.19 alarm: 400 ppm in 4–15 min, 150 ppm in 10–50 min, 70 ppm in 60–240 min (First Alert CO710; Kidde KN-COB-DP2CA)
Quiet at low steady levels: built not to sound at 30 ppm, and Kidde's Nighthawk wasn't investigated below 70 ppm; 100 ppm for 4 hours can cause headaches (First Alert CO710; Kidde Nighthawk)
Senses CO only at the alarm itself, and does not detect smoke, fire or any other gas (Intertek CSA 6.19; Kidde Nighthawk)
Rated about 4.4–37.8 °C: keep it out of unheated garages, porches and attics; cold weakens the battery (Kidde Nighthawk; Kidde temperature)
At high levels, alcohols, solvents, hydrogen and hydrogen sulphide can damage the sensor or cause false readings (Kidde Nighthawk)
identify: Says Carbon Monoxide or CO on the front or label; combination units also say smoke. Canadian alarms carry a mark referring to CSA 6.19 (Health Canada CO); US ones list UL 2034 (First Alert CO710). Kidde's Canadian KN-COB-DP2CA uses an electrochemical sensor and sounds 4 short beeps, a 5-second pause, then 4 beeps again for CO (Kidde KN-COB-DP2CA). Look for the 'Replace by' date: CSA 6.19 requires that marking and, since 2021, an audible end-of-life signal that repeats every 30–60 seconds (Intertek CSA 6.19). The alarms checked here are rated for 7 or 10 years (Kidde Nighthawk; Kidde KN-COB-DP2CA; First Alert CO710). Digital models show ppm and keep a peak reading (First Alert CO710). Chirps are not the alarm and differ by maker. On the Kidde Nighthawk, one chirp every 15 seconds means low battery, one every 30 seconds with a flashing red light means a fault, and after 7 years it chirps every 30 seconds to say replace it (Kidde Nighthawk). On the First Alert CO710, 3 chirps a minute means a fault, and 5 chirps a minute with End on the screen means end of life (First Alert CO710).
test: 1. Date: read the 'Replace by' or install date. Past it, the sensor may no longer detect CO accurately (Kidde Nighthawk): treat it as unreliable. 2. Power: fit fresh batteries of the type marked. Sealed 10-year alarms can't take new ones, so once flat they must be replaced (First Alert CO710). A hardwired alarm's 9 V backup is only meant for short power cuts (Kidde Nighthawk). 3. Press the test button: a Kidde Nighthawk gives 4 beeps, a pause and 4 beeps with a flashing red light; a First Alert CO710 shows tst (Kidde Nighthawk; First Alert CO710). This checks the electronics, power and horn only. It makes no CO, so it can't prove the sensor still works (First Alert test; Kidde KN-COB-DP2CA). 4. Fail signs: no sound or a weak one, Err or End on the screen, a steady red light, or trouble chirps that fresh batteries don't stop (First Alert CO710; Kidde Nighthawk). An alarm that fails its test must be replaced (First Alert CO710). Don't try to test the sensor with exhaust, smoke or a fire; First Alert says never create dangerous conditions to test a CO alarm (First Alert test). 5. Mount it in or near sleeping areas, not in kitchens, garages or furnace rooms (Kidde Nighthawk).

decay.note: Estimate. Sensors are rated 7 or 10 years from power-up (Kidde Nighthawk; First Alert CO710). Alarms in place are spread across that span, many already past it, and sealed batteries can't be changed.

improvise: There is no safe stand-in for a working CO alarm where people sleep. A combustion analyser or CO meter reads CO, but is not built to be left on as an alarm: testo says its 310 must not be used as a safety alarm device (testo 310). A multi-gas monitor with a CO sensor does alarm, while its battery and sensor last. Without any detector, run generators outdoors at least 6 m from buildings with the exhaust pointed away from windows and doors (Health Canada CO), and burn nothing indoors without a sound flue. Watch flames: yellow means fuel isn't burning completely and CO may be present, but a blue flame doesn't clear a burner, since a broken furnace heat exchanger or a blocked flue can also put CO in the house (First Alert CO710). You can't see or smell CO (Intertek CSA 6.19). Know the signs: headache, tiredness, drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, trouble thinking; victims often know they feel ill but get too muddled to escape (Intertek CSA 6.19). Get everyone outside at once. An expired alarm may not respond to CO: Kidde says a unit giving its end-of-life signal will not respond to CO (Kidde Nighthawk), and the test button can't show the sensor works. If it is all you have, hang it as an extra, but its silence means nothing: keep burners out of the house and watch for symptoms. A CO alarm is not a smoke alarm (Kidde Nighthawk).

buildings.loc: hallway ceiling or wall outside bedrooms, plugged into a low outlet, or as a combined smoke/CO unit
safety aisle beside smoke alarms and fire extinguishers
inside suites near bedrooms, and in corridors heated by gas furnaces
inside RVs and trailers near the sleeping area, and the parts counter
guest-room ceilings and corridors near fuel-burning equipment
corridors near resident rooms and the boiler room door
